risk.rationale: SupportBot is a customer-support chatbot for a home energy web shop. It answers questions about orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs, and it hands over to a human on request. It interacts directly with people and generates text with an LLM, so the Art. 50(1) transparency duty applies. It makes no decisions about people. It does not do credit scoring, eligibility assessment or any other Annex III use, and it doesn't do any Art. 5 practice. Complaint decisions, contract changes and advice are out of scope. The code has an open TODO (SUP-88) to label AI replies, so Art. 50 compliance is not yet complete. The privacy notice does say replies are AI-generated. The system is not high-risk, so limited is the right tier.
triggers: Art. 50(1): chatbot interacting directly with natural persons
Art. 50(2): LLM-generated text content (labelling TODO SUP-88 open)

requirements.title: No prohibited AI practices
requirements.statement: The system does not implement any practice prohibited by Art. 5(1): subliminal or manipulative techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, crime prediction based solely on profiling, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference in the workplace or in education, or biometric categorisation inferring sensitive traits.

checks.description: no emotion recognition / social scoring / face scraping code

requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code or documentation showing the system infers emotions (e.g. from video interviews or voice) of employees/candidates/students, scores people on social behaviour, scrapes facial images, or categorises people by biometrics into sensitive traits. A comment or doc stating that such a feature is NOT implemented is evidence of compliance, not a violation. Mark non_compliant only if a prohibited practice is actually implemented or planned for production.

requirements.title: Risk classification documented
requirements.statement: The provider documents the AI Act risk classification of the system with its rationale: the applicable Annex III area/point if high-risk, the Art. 6(3) assessment if an Annex III system is claimed not to be high-risk, or why the system is limited/minimal risk.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a README section, ADR or compliance document that states the risk tier AND gives a reason (e.g. "Annex III point 4(a) recruitment", "chatbot, transparency obligations under Art. 50", "spam filtering, no Annex III use case"). A bare marketing claim ("fully compliant") is not a classification.

requirements.title: Risk management system documented
requirements.statement: A risk management process is documented for the high-risk system: known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety and fundamental rights are identified and evaluated, and targeted mitigation measures with residual-risk acceptance are recorded and kept up to date.

checks.description: a risk assessment / risk register document exists

requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a risk register / risk assessment / model risk management document listing concrete risks (e.g. discrimination, automation bias, data drift), their likelihood/impact and mitigations. A single sentence like "risks are low" is not sufficient (partial at most).

requirements.title: Training data documented (datasheet)
requirements.statement: Training, validation and test data sets are documented: origin and collection process, original purpose for personal data, preparation steps (labelling, cleaning, enrichment), assumptions, and the availability/quantity/suitability of the data.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a datasheet / data card / training-data document. Code that loads a CSV is not documentation. Partial if only some of origin, preparation and splits are described.

requirements.title: Bias examination and mitigation of data sets
requirements.statement: The data sets have been examined for possible biases likely to lead to discrimination (including representativeness for the persons and setting the system is used on), and measures to detect, prevent and mitigate the identified biases are documented with results.
requirements.llm_guidance: Requires an actual bias/fairness analysis with results (metrics per group, findings, mitigations). A plan ("bias audit planned"), a TODO, or merely excluding protected attributes from the features does NOT satisfy this requirement on its own (proxies may remain). Judge from documents and evaluation code/reports.

requirements.title: Technical documentation (Annex IV)
requirements.statement: Technical documentation covering the Annex IV elements exists before deployment: general description and intended purpose, versions, how the system interacts with other software, development methods, design specifications and key design choices, system architecture, and validation/testing procedures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if a document (or set of docs) covers most Annex IV(1)-(2) elements. An architecture overview plus a model card without development/validation information is partial.

requirements.title: Model card for the deployed model
requirements.statement: A model card documents the deployed model: intended use and out-of-scope uses, version, training data summary, evaluation results, capabilities and known limitations.
requirements.llm_guidance: Check that a model card exists and covers intended use, limitations and evaluation results.

requirements.title: Instructions for use for deployers
requirements.statement: Instructions for use are provided to deployers and contain at least: provider identity and contact, intended purpose, level of accuracy and its metrics, known limitations and foreseeable misuse risks, human oversight measures, and how to collect and interpret the logs.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if the instructions contain all the listed elements. If a guide exists but misses accuracy metrics, limitations or log interpretation, the status is partial. Sections marked TBD count as missing.

requirements.title: Interpretable outputs for deployers
requirements.statement: The system provides information that lets deployers interpret each output (e.g. main reasons, feature contributions, reason codes or confidence) rather than a bare score.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that returns explanations/reason codes alongside the score and shows them to the human reviewer. A global feature-importance chart in a notebook alone is partial.

requirements.title: Disclosure of interaction with an AI system
requirements.statement: Natural persons interacting directly with the AI system (e.g. a chatbot) are informed, clearly and at the latest at the first interaction, that they are interacting with an AI system.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for user-facing UI strings (React/HTML templates, chat greeting) that tell users they talk to an AI, shown at the start of the conversation. A statement buried in terms of service is not sufficient.
evidence_queries: you are chatting with an AI

requirements.title: Marking of AI-generated content
requirements.statement: Synthetic text, image, audio or video generated by the system is marked as AI-generated in a machine-readable format (and labelled for the recipient where it is published or delivered).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that adds an AI-generated flag/header/metadata or visible label to each generated message. A TODO or ticket reference to add labelling later means non_compliant. A disclosure that the user talks to an AI (Art. 50(1)) is a different obligation and does not mark the content.

requirements.title: Affected persons informed about high-risk AI use
requirements.statement: Natural persons subject to decisions made or assisted by the high-risk AI system (candidates, applicants, workers) are informed that such a system is used on them.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a candidate/applicant notice, privacy notice or e-mail template that tells the person an AI system is used to assess them. Recruiter-facing UI text does not inform the candidate.

requirements.title: Automatic logging of AI decisions
requirements.statement: The system automatically records an event for each decision/output over its lifetime, with timestamp, input reference, output, model version and (where applicable) the human reviewer, enabling traceability and post-market monitoring.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for code that writes a structured record for every prediction (custom journal/audit classes count). Commented-out logging calls, TODOs or debug prints do not count. Logging only errors is not decision logging.

requirements.title: Logs retained for at least six months
requirements.statement: Automatically generated decision logs are retained for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and of at least six months (>= 180 days).
requirements.llm_guidance: Find the effective retention of the decision/audit logs (config, Terraform log group, lifecycle rules). Compliant only if >= 180 days. If logs exist but retention is shorter or unbounded deletion is configured, non_compliant. If no logs exist at all, non_compliant.

requirements.title: Human can override or disregard the AI output
requirements.statement: Natural persons overseeing the system can decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse an individual output of the system, and the override is recorded.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an implemented mechanism (API endpoint, UI action, workflow state) letting a human change the outcome. A flag set to False, a README promise without code, or an override limited to admins for model config does not count.

requirements.title: Stop / interrupt mechanism
requirements.statement: Operators can interrupt the system (a 'stop' button, kill switch or similar procedure) so that it halts in a safe state, e.g. automated processing is suspended and cases fall back to manual handling.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept any implemented switch (feature flag, admin endpoint, config) that stops automated decisions and routes work to humans. Infrastructure scaling to zero without a documented procedure is partial.

requirements.title: No adverse decision solely on the AI output
requirements.statement: Decisions adverse to natural persons (e.g. rejection, decline) are not taken automatically on the basis of the AI output alone; a competent human reviews and confirms them, mitigating automation bias.
requirements.llm_guidance: Trace the decision flow in code. If any adverse outcome is set without a human step (e.g. score below threshold -> rejected), it is non_compliant; if only a subset of cases gets human review (e.g. above an amount threshold), partial.

requirements.title: Accuracy levels and metrics declared
requirements.statement: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics (e.g. AUC, precision/recall, error rates) are declared in the documentation accompanying the system (instructions for use and/or model card).
requirements.llm_guidance: Metrics must be declared in documentation shipped with the system, with values. A training script that prints accuracy is not a declaration.

requirements.title: Resilience to errors (fallback / fail-safe)
requirements.statement: The system handles errors, faults and model unavailability safely (e.g. timeouts and exceptions lead to a fail-safe outcome such as routing to manual handling, never to an automatic adverse decision).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for explicit error handling around model inference with a safe fallback. Generic web framework error pages are not sufficient.

requirements.title: Input validation against malformed or adversarial inputs
requirements.statement: Inputs to the model are validated (schema, types, ranges, size limits, file types) before inference to resist malformed or adversarial inputs.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for schema validation (pydantic/zod/marshmallow), constraints and upload limits on the inference path. Reading raw request bodies directly into the model is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Protection of model endpoints against unauthorised use
requirements.statement: Inference and model-management endpoints are protected against unauthorised third parties (authentication and authorisation), so that the system's use, outputs or performance cannot be altered by exploiting vulnerabilities.
requirements.llm_guidance: Every inference and admin route must require authentication; admin/model routes need authorisation. Partial if some sensitive routes are unauthenticated.

requirements.title: Quality management and post-market monitoring procedures
requirements.statement: Documented procedures cover change management of the model/system, validation before release, post-market monitoring of performance in production (e.g. drift), and serious-incident reporting.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if the repository documents change management, pre-release validation, production monitoring AND incident reporting; partial if only some are covered.

requirements.title: Testing against predefined metrics before release
requirements.statement: The system is tested before release against prior defined metrics and thresholds appropriate to its intended purpose (e.g. an automated quality gate failing the build below a minimum AUC).
requirements.llm_guidance: Smoke tests that only check an HTTP 200 are not model validation; require assertions against metric thresholds on held-out data.

requirements.title: Lawful basis documented for each processing purpose
requirements.statement: Each purpose for which personal data is processed has a documented lawful basis under Art. 6(1) (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests), and consent is collected and recorded where it is the basis relied on.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for a privacy notice, record of processing or DPIA naming the lawful basis per purpose. A README claim "fully GDPR compliant" is not evidence of a lawful basis.

requirements.title: Privacy notice provided to data subjects
requirements.statement: Data subjects receive a privacy notice at collection stating the controller and contact details, purposes and lawful basis, recipients, retention period, and their rights (access, rectification, erasure, objection, complaint).
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if a notice covering controller, purposes, legal basis, retention and rights exists and is shown/linked to data subjects. Partial if key items (e.g. retention or rights) are missing.
evidence_queries: how long we keep your data

requirements.title: Storage limitation enforced
requirements.statement: Personal data is kept no longer than necessary for its purpose: a retention period proportionate to the purpose is defined for each data category and enforced automatically (TTL, purge job, lifecycle rule).
requirements.llm_guidance: Check both that a retention period is defined AND enforced in code/IaC, and that it is proportionate (e.g. keeping raw support chats for years without justification is excessive; keeping data "forever" is non_compliant). Defined and enforced but disproportionate -> partial.

requirements.title: Right to erasure implemented
requirements.statement: A mechanism exists to erase a data subject's personal data on request without undue delay (endpoint, admin job or documented procedure covering all stores, including derived data).
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an implemented deletion path for a single data subject. Automatic expiry of all data after N days is not an on-request erasure mechanism (partial at most).

requirements.title: Safeguards for solely automated decisions
requirements.statement: Decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects are not based solely on automated processing, or, where an Art. 22(2) exception applies, the data subject can obtain human intervention, express their point of view and contest the decision.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant if no significant decision is fully automated, OR if automated decisions come with an implemented contest/appeal path leading to human review. Non_compliant if decisions are fully automated with no recourse.

requirements.title: Meaningful information about the logic involved
requirements.statement: Data subjects are informed of the existence of automated decision-making/profiling and receive meaningful information about the logic involved and its envisaged consequences.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for an applicant/candidate-facing explanation of the main factors used and the consequences. Internal model documentation does not inform data subjects.

requirements.title: Data minimisation and privacy by design
requirements.statement: Only personal data necessary for the purpose is collected and used (no unnecessary sensitive or protected attributes as model features), and privacy-by-design measures such as pseudonymisation or redaction are applied before processing or sharing with third parties.
requirements.llm_guidance: Inspect model features and data flows. Using gender/age/nationality as features, or sending raw personal data to a third-party LLM without redaction, is non_compliant. Look for explicit redaction/pseudonymisation code.

requirements.title: Encryption of personal data at rest and in transit
requirements.statement: Personal data is encrypted at rest (databases, object storage, volumes, backups) and in transit (TLS) as appropriate to the risk.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both at-rest and in-transit encryption must be evidenced for all stores holding personal data. Only one of the two -> partial. Self-signed dev certificates in docker-compose do not count for production.

requirements.title: Access control to personal data
requirements.statement: Access to personal data and to administrative functions is restricted to authenticated and authorised personnel (authentication, role-based authorisation, least privilege).
requirements.llm_guidance: Check that endpoints exposing personal data require authentication and that admin/export routes check roles. Unauthenticated upload/listing endpoints are non_compliant.

requirements.title: Record of processing activities
requirements.statement: A record of processing activities is maintained for the system listing purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients, transfers, retention limits and security measures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Accept a ROPA entry in the repo (markdown/yaml). A DPIA or privacy notice alone is not a ROPA but may be partial if it contains the Art. 30(1) items.

requirements.title: Data protection impact assessment
requirements.statement: A DPIA has been carried out for the processing (systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing) and contains a description of the processing, necessity and proportionality assessment, risk assessment and mitigation measures.
requirements.llm_guidance: Compliant only if a DPIA document with the Art. 35(7) elements exists.

requirements.title: AI use disclosed in user interfaces
requirements.statement: Every interface where a person interacts with the AI system or sees an AI-produced score, ranking, classification or text visibly discloses AI involvement; decision-support UIs state that the output is an AI recommendation and who decides.
requirements.llm_guidance: Inspect UI components, e-mail templates and notification texts. Neutral names like "Smart Score" do not disclose AI involvement.

requirements.title: AI-generated content labelled
requirements.statement: AI-generated text/media delivered to customers carries a visible "AI-generated" label and, where feasible, a machine-readable marker.
requirements.llm_guidance: A banner saying the user chats with an AI is POL-1, not POL-2. Look for per-message labelling or metadata. TODO comments do not count.

requirements.title: Prediction logging with 180-day retention
requirements.statement: Every production prediction/response is logged with timestamp, correlation id, model version, input reference and output, in tamper-resistant storage retained for at least 180 days.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both parts are needed: structured per-prediction logging AND >= 180 days retention. Logging with shorter retention -> partial. No logging -> non_compliant.
evidence_queries: prediction log model version request id

requirements.title: Raw personal-data inputs deleted within 30 days
requirements.statement: Raw inputs containing personal data (documents, messages, transcripts, payloads) are automatically deleted or anonymised within 30 days, unless a documented legal retention obligation applies.
requirements.llm_guidance: Find the retention of each raw-input store. Any raw store kept > 30 days without a documented legal obligation is non_compliant; no automated deletion at all is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Encryption at rest and TLS in transit
requirements.statement: Storage of personal data, model artefacts and logs is encrypted at rest, and all service traffic uses TLS 1.2+.
requirements.llm_guidance: Both at rest and in transit must be shown; one of the two -> partial.

requirements.title: Access control on model endpoints
requirements.statement: Inference and model-management endpoints require authentication (or are declared public and rate-limited), and administrative endpoints enforce role-based authorisation.
requirements.llm_guidance: Enumerate routes. Any undeclared unauthenticated inference/upload route, or an admin route without a role check, is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Human approval of adverse decisions
requirements.statement: Adverse decisions about natural persons (rejection, decline, closure) are approved by a human reviewer who sees the AI output and reasons and can change the outcome, and the approval is logged.
requirements.llm_guidance: Trace adverse outcomes in code. Human approval for only part of the cases (e.g. above an amount threshold) is partial. Automatic rejection is non_compliant.

requirements.title: Model card for every deployed model
requirements.statement: Each deployed model (including third-party models) has a model card covering intended and out-of-scope use, version, training data summary, evaluation metrics, limitations and owner.
requirements.llm_guidance: Check presence and completeness of the model card(s) against the listed fields.

requirements.title: Rate limiting on AI endpoints
requirements.statement: AI endpoints reachable from untrusted networks enforce per-client rate limiting configured in code or configuration.
requirements.llm_guidance: Look for rate-limit middleware (express-rate-limit, slowapi), gateway throttling or ingress annotations. Public endpoints without it are non_compliant.

requirements.title: AI incident response procedure
requirements.statement: The repository contains an AI incident response procedure (detection, escalation, reporting) that requires reporting serious incidents to the AI Governance Board within 24 hours.
requirements.llm_guidance: A generic ops runbook without AI incidents or without the 24h governance reporting is partial.

requirements.title: Bias and fairness evaluation before release
requirements.statement: A documented bias and fairness evaluation (metrics and results per protected group, mitigations) exists for the released model and is referenced from the model card.
requirements.llm_guidance: Requires actual results. "Planned", TODOs or excluding protected features only is non_compliant.

verdicts.rationale: The evidence shows SupportBot is a customer-support chatbot for orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs (E1, E3). The system prompt limits it to those topics (E6). The chat flow in E7 and the widget in E5 show no emotion inference, social scoring, face scraping, biometric categorisation, or manipulative or vulnerability-exploiting techniques. The README states it takes no decisions about people (E3). The excerpts are partial and the repository was not fully reviewed, so confidence is not higher.
gaps: No explicit statement that Art. 5 prohibited practices are not implemented
Excerpts are truncated and do not cover the whole codebase (e.g. retrieval, transcripts, analytics)
verdicts.remediation: Add an Art. 5 screening note to the README or an ADR. It should state that SupportBot does no emotion inference, social scoring, biometric categorisation or facial-image scraping, and uses no manipulative techniques. Add a CI check that flags related code, such as sentiment or emotion analysis of customers.

verdicts.rationale: The README "AI Act position" section [E1] states the risk tier (limited-risk) and gives reasons: the system is a chatbot that interacts directly with customers, it takes no decisions about people, and it is not in any Annex III area. It also names the Art. 50 transparency obligations that apply. This matches the guidance example for a chatbot. The model card [E2] supports the classification by limiting the intended use to support Q&A and excluding complaint decisions and contract changes. The classification is brief and has no standalone assessment document, but the requirement asks only for the tier and a rationale.
gaps: Rationale is brief; no dated or owner-approved classification record
No explicit walk-through of the Annex III areas
Art. 50(2) labelling of AI-generated output is still a TODO in E3 (separate requirement)
verdicts.remediation: Add a short docs/ai-act-classification.md or an ADR. It should record the date, owner and approver, and it should check the system against each Annex III area (for example, that it does no profiling or creditworthiness scoring). It should also state the limited-risk conclusion with its Art. 50 obligations and say when the classification will be reviewed.

E1 shows the ChatWidget renders a persistent header disclosure, "You are chatting with an AI assistant", as soon as the widget loads, before the user sends anything. That meets the Art. 50(1) and 50(5) requirement to inform users at or before the first interaction, in clear user-facing UI text. The privacy notice (E3) and README (E2) back this up but are not what the conclusion rests on. The TODO in E4 concerns labelling AI-generated output under Art. 50(2). That is a different requirement and does not affect this one.
gaps: Accessibility of the disclosure (e.g. ARIA role/live region, contrast) is not shown in the evidence
The first bot greeting message does not itself mention AI; the disclosure relies on the header text
verdicts.remediation: Optionally add role="note" or aria-live to the disclosure paragraph in ChatWidget.tsx and verify it meets accessibility requirements. Consider including the AI statement in the initial bot greeting. Track the separate Art. 50(2) output-labelling TODO (SUP-88).

verdicts.rationale: The reply path in server/src/llm.ts returns only text, model, handover and usage. It adds no AI-generated flag, header or metadata. It also contains an explicit TODO (SUP-88) to label AI-generated replies later, which the guidance treats as non_compliant (E1). The chat widget shows a banner saying the user is talking to an AI, but that is an Art. 50(1) disclosure. It does not mark the content, and individual bot messages carry no label or machine-readable marker (E4). The privacy notice and README likewise only disclose AI use (E2, E3). The logs record model calls but do not mark the outputs (E10, E12).
gaps: No machine-readable AI-generated marker (flag, header, metadata) on generated replies
No per-message visible label in the widget
Labelling is only a TODO (SUP-88)
Only a general Art. 50(1) disclosure exists, which does not mark content
verdicts.remediation: In server/src/llm.ts, add a field such as `aiGenerated: true` (with model and provider) to the Reply type. Return it from /api/chat, and also set a response header such as `X-AI-Generated: true`. Persist it in transcript_messages as well. In web/src/components/ChatWidget.tsx, carry the flag in the Msg type and render a visible "AI-generated" badge on each bot message. Use a simple text label now rather than waiting for the design badge, and close SUP-88. Document the marking approach in docs/, including any C2PA or metadata approach for exported or published content.

The privacy notice (E1) names a lawful basis for each processing purpose. Support chat rests on Art. 6(1)(b), and quality improvement and complaint handling rest on Art. 6(1)(f). The RoPA entry (E2) lists the same three purposes: customer support, quality assurance and complaint handling. No purpose relies on consent, so no consent collection is needed. Small gaps remain: the RoPA doesn't record the lawful basis per purpose, and there is no documented legitimate-interests assessment for the (f) purposes.
gaps: RoPA entry (E2) does not list the lawful basis per purpose
No documented legitimate interests assessment (LIA) for quality improvement
Prospective customers listed as data subjects (E2) may not have a contract, so Art. 6(1)(b) may not fit them unless pre-contractual steps apply
verdicts.remediation: Add a 'Lawful basis' column to docs/ropa.md that maps each purpose to its Art. 6(1) basis. Add a short legitimate interests assessment (purpose, necessity, balancing test) for quality assurance and complaint handling. Clarify the basis for prospective customers who use the chat without a contract.

verdicts.rationale: E1 is a privacy notice that names the controller and contact details (and a DPO contact). It states purposes with legal bases (Art. 6(1)(b) and (f)) and recipients (OpenAI as processor, the customer-care team). It gives the retention period (2 years) and lists the rights: access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, portability and complaint to a supervisory authority. E4 shows the chat widget links to the notice at the point of collection, next to the AI disclosure. E2 corroborates the controller, recipients, transfers and retention details.
gaps: Notice does not spell out the legitimate interest pursued for Art. 6(1)(f) (Art. 13(1)(d))
No statement on whether providing data is a statutory or contractual requirement (Art. 13(2)(e))
No explicit statement on third-country transfers (E2 says none outside the EEA)
Not verified that /privacy#support-chat serves docs/privacy.md
verdicts.remediation: Update docs/privacy.md to describe the legitimate interest behind the Art. 6(1)(f) processing. Add a line saying no transfers outside the EEA take place and a line on whether providing data is required. Confirm the /privacy#support-chat anchor renders this notice.

verdicts.rationale: Retention is defined and documented: transcripts 730 days in config/app.yaml (E4), logs 90 days (E4, E6). A nightly purge job is shown in E1, which is truncated, so the wiring to cfg.retention.transcript_days and whether it is actually started can't be confirmed. The 2-year period has a stated purpose (QA, complaints), but it is long for free-text chats that may contain contact and contract data, and no further justification is given. Raw messages are stored unredacted (E1, E8). Log retention of 90 days is only stated in config, and Terraform shows only 7-day backups (E2), with no enforcement evidence for Loki. Enforcement is likely but not fully verified, and proportionality is questionable.
gaps: Excerpt of startRetentionJob is truncated; unclear it is invoked in index.ts with cfg.retention.transcript_days
Proportionality of 2-year retention of unredacted chat content not justified (e.g. no shorter period for raw text or anonymisation after QA)
No IaC or config showing enforcement of the 90-day Loki log retention
chat_sessions and other personal data categories have no defined retention period
Retention period not shown to data subjects (Art.13(2)(a)), no privacy notice evidence
verdicts.remediation: Confirm startRetentionJob(cfg.retention.transcript_days) is called at startup, and add a test for it. Extend the purge to chat_sessions. Document a retention schedule per data category with a justification. Consider a shorter period for raw transcripts, or redact or anonymise them after QA sampling. Add Loki retention (limits_config.retention_period or compactor) as code. Publish the retention periods in the privacy notice.

verdicts.rationale: E1 has deleteCustomerData(customerId), which deletes transcript_messages and chat_sessions rows for one customer. E5 says erasure is restricted to the support-admin role, and E3 imports the function into the server. However, the E3 excerpt is truncated and shows only the admin export route, not a route or job that calls deleteCustomerData. The function covers only two tables. It does not cover application logs in Loki, which are keyed by sessionId (E12, E9), or backups (E13, 7-day retention). It also does not cover data sent to OpenAI, though E11 says that provider keeps no data. Anonymous sessions with a null customer_id cannot be erased by customer ID. No documented erasure procedure or timeline is shown. The automatic 2-year purge (E1, E2, E9) is expiry, not on-request erasure.
gaps: No visible endpoint or job that invokes deleteCustomerData (E3 excerpt is truncated)
No documented erasure procedure or response timeline
Logs in Loki keyed by sessionId are not covered by erasure
Backups (7-day retention) are not addressed
Anonymous sessions (customer_id null) cannot be erased by customer ID
Derived data and data held at the processor are not addressed
Data subjects have no self-service route and no documented identity verification
verdicts.remediation: Expose an authenticated admin route, for example DELETE /admin/customers/:customerId, that calls deleteCustomerData and writes an audit entry. Also support erasure by session ID for anonymous users. Extend deletion to the logs, any other stores such as embeddings or caches, and the backup lifecycle. Add a docs/erasure-procedure.md that covers identity verification, a one-month deadline, the stores covered, and the processor notification. Add tests for the deletion path.

Raw customer messages are sent to the third-party LLM with no redaction. E4 says messages go to the provider "as typed" and that redaction of contact details was evaluated and postponed. E6 passes the raw message and history straight into the OpenAI call. E7 stores full text, which may include email, phone and address, with no minimisation. E2 confirms free text may contain contact and contract data. Some safeguards exist: an EU processor with zero retention (E4), encryption (E8), a retention limit and an input length cap (E10), and no protected attributes appear as features. None of these replaces the missing pseudonymisation or redaction that the requirement asks for before sharing with a third party.
gaps: No PII redaction or pseudonymisation before sending messages to OpenAI
Transcripts stored unredacted, including contact details
Redaction explicitly postponed (ADR 0001)
No documented data-minimisation assessment for the chat history sent to the LLM
Customer id is stored with the content and is not pseudonymised
verdicts.remediation: Add a redaction step in server/src/llm.ts and transcripts.ts that detects emails, phone numbers, addresses, IBANs and contract numbers (regex plus NER). Replace them with reversible placeholders such as [EMAIL_1], keeping the mapping server-side. Apply it to the message, the history and the stored transcripts. Evaluate delivery-question quality with placeholders, since the order id can be kept as a token. Update ADR 0001 and the RoPA with the result, and add tests for the redaction.

verdicts.rationale: The main personal-data store is the RDS Postgres transcripts DB. It has storage_encrypted=true with a rotating KMS key and a force-ssl parameter group (E1). The app connects with TLS and certificate verification (rejectUnauthorized: true) (E8). The public API has a TLS ingress with a Let's Encrypt production issuer and ssl-redirect (E3). The RoPA lists TLS and KMS-encrypted RDS as security measures (E2). RDS encrypts automated backups and snapshots when storage is encrypted, so backups are covered. Residual gaps: there is no explicit evidence for other stores such as logs, and no evidence for TLS on the LLM provider call, which is not shown. The ingress-to-pod hop is not shown to be encrypted.
gaps: No evidence on encryption at rest for application logs or other stores that may hold personal data
In-cluster TLS (ingress to pod) not shown
Outbound TLS to the LLM provider not evidenced in the excerpts
Backup encryption is implied by RDS encryption but not explicit
verdicts.remediation: Document that RDS automated backups and snapshots inherit KMS encryption. Confirm that log storage is encrypted at rest. Document TLS for the ingress-to-pod hop (for example a service mesh or backend-protocol HTTPS) and for the LLM API calls. Add these to docs/ropa.md or a security-measures document.

verdicts.rationale: E1 shows real authentication: sessionAuth verifies a signed session token, and requireAdmin verifies an RS256 SSO token and checks the `support-admin` role, returning 403 otherwise. E6 applies sessionAuth to /api/chat and requireAdmin to the admin transcript export route. E2 claims "admin RBAC". The E6 excerpt is truncated, so the admin erasure route and any other routes can't be confirmed to be protected. Least privilege is only partly shown: the chat history lookup is scoped by session id (E4), but nothing shows that a customer can only reach their own data, and there is no evidence on database-level access or on staff access reviews. Because the export and delete functions in E4 do no authorisation themselves, they rely entirely on route-level middleware.
gaps: E6 is truncated, so protection of the admin erasure route can't be verified
No evidence of least-privilege scoping, such as database roles or a single support-admin role covering all admin functions
No evidence of access reviews, audit logging of admin access, or staff authorisation procedures
Session tokens are bearer tokens only, with no evidence of binding or expiry
Authorisation is not enforced inside the data-access functions, which export and delete by customerId
verdicts.remediation: Confirm that every admin route (export, erasure, any listing) uses requireAdmin, and add tests that assert 401 and 403 responses. Add finer-grained roles, for example separate export and erase permissions. Log admin access to personal data with the actor's identity. Restrict database credentials to the minimum privileges needed. Document access-control and review procedures in docs, for example in an access-control policy. Set an expiry on session tokens.

verdicts.rationale: E1 (docs/ropa.md) is a dedicated ROPA entry (PA-CC-07) covering the Art. 30(1) items. It names the controller and DPO contact, the purposes, data subjects and personal data categories, and recipients (including OpenAI as processor). It also records transfers (none outside the EEA), erasure limits (transcripts 2 years, logs 90 days) and security measures. The retention limits match E9 and E3. The security measures match E10 (KMS encryption, SSL) and E9 (rate limiting). E4 confirms the record is part of the docs set.
gaps: Controller contact details limited to the DPO email; no postal address or phone in the ROPA entry (the postal address appears only in E3)
No review date or owner for the ROPA entry
No joint controller or representative statement (may not apply)
Transfers entry does not address OpenAI sub-processors or US support access
verdicts.remediation: Add the controller's address and contact details to docs/ropa.md. Add a last-reviewed date and an entry owner. State explicitly whether there is a joint controller or representative. Confirm the 'no transfers' claim against OpenAI's sub-processors and support access. Reference the logging/Loki and backup retention (7 days) in the erasure and security rows.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to high risk systems; this system is classified as limited.

The only AI-facing interface is the chat widget. In E2 it shows a visible header disclosure ("You are chatting with an AI assistant. It can make mistakes; ask for a human agent at any time"). It appears before the first interaction and isn't hidden in a tooltip or the terms of service. E3 and E4 support this. The system is a customer chatbot and not decision support, so the "AI recommendation and who decides" clause doesn't apply (E4). The TODO in E1 about labelling individual replies is a server-side note. The Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking it refers to is a different requirement from this UI disclosure.
gaps: No per-message AI label on bot replies (open TODO SUP-88)
E-mail templates and other notification channels were not in the evidence, so they could not be checked
verdicts.remediation: Complete SUP-88 by adding an "AI" badge to each bot message in ChatWidget.tsx. Confirm that no e-mail or notification templates carry AI-generated text without disclosure. Keep the header disclosure in place.

verdicts.rationale: No per-message AI-generated label or machine-readable marker is implemented. The ChatWidget (E2) only has a general header disclosure ("You are chatting with an AI assistant"), which is a POL-1 banner and not a per-reply label. Bot messages are rendered as plain text with no badge. The server's answer() (E1) returns no AI-generated flag or metadata, and the only reference is a TODO(SUP-88) saying labelling is still to be done, which does not count. The privacy notice and README (E5, E4) describe AI use but do not label content.
gaps: No visible 'AI-generated' badge on each bot reply in ChatWidget
No machine-readable marker (response header or metadata field) in the /api/chat response
Labelling is only a TODO (SUP-88) in llm.ts
Header banner covers chat disclosure (POL-1) but not per-message labelling (POL-2)
verdicts.remediation: In web/src/components/ChatWidget.tsx, render an "AI-generated" badge next to each message with from === "bot", excluding handover messages written by humans. In server/src/llm.ts and the /api/chat route, add a field such as aiGenerated: true to the Reply payload and set a response header such as X-AI-Generated: true. Store the flag in transcript_messages metadata. Remove the TODO once this is done, and add a test that asserts both the label and the marker.

verdicts.rationale: Structured per-call logging exists (E1, E2, E3) with epoch timestamp, sessionId (usable as correlation id) and model_version. However, it omits an input reference and the output itself. The only thing it records about the output is the completion token count. The raw messages are stored in a separate Postgres transcript table (E8), but that table is not linked to the log entries. Log retention is configured at 90 days (E5), below the required 180. The transcripts table is a mutable table that has deletion functions (E8), so it is not tamper-resistant. No append-only or immutability control and no waiver are shown. The 730-day transcript retention does not satisfy the log retention requirement.
gaps: Log retention is 90 days, below the 180-day minimum, and no waiver is shown
The log does not record the output or an output reference
The log has no input reference such as an input hash or record id
There is no dedicated correlation or request id, only sessionId
No tamper-resistant or append-only protection for the logs
No reviewer identity or action is logged when a human takes over (handover)
The transcript table is mutable and deletable, and it is not linked to the log entries
verdicts.remediation: Set logging.retention_days to at least 180 in config/app.yaml and make the Loki retention match. Ship the logs to append-only or WORM storage, for example S3 Object Lock. Extend LlmCall and logLlmCall to include a request id, an input hash or transcript message id, and the output or an output hash or id. Log the reviewer identity and action on handover. If shorter retention is intended, document an approved waiver.

verdicts.rationale: Raw chat transcripts contain personal data (E1, E3). An automated nightly purge exists (E1), but it is driven by config retention.transcript_days: 730 (E5). The privacy notice and RoPA also state 2 years (E7, E3). That is far beyond 30 days. The only justification given is QA and complaint handling (E5, E1), not a documented legal retention obligation. Application logs are kept 90 days (E5, E3). They hold session ids and metadata rather than raw message content (E6, E12), so they are secondary. The deterministic check for a retention value of 30 days or less finds none.
gaps: Transcript retention is 730 days, above the 30-day limit
No documented legal retention obligation; QA and complaint handling are not legal obligations
No anonymisation of transcripts before the 2-year purge
Raw messages are sent to the LLM provider unredacted (E11), and redaction was postponed
RDS backups kept 7 days (E13) are minor and not addressed in the retention schedule
verdicts.remediation: Set retention.transcript_days to 30 or less in config/app.yaml, and make startRetentionJob in server/src/transcripts.ts use it. Update docs/ropa.md and docs/privacy.md to match. If longer retention is needed for QA or disputes, irreversibly anonymise or redact PII from messages at 30 days and keep only the anonymised data. Where a real legal obligation applies, document it in a retention schedule that cites the legal basis. Add a test or monitor that confirms the purge job runs.

verdicts.rationale: Encryption at rest is shown for the transcripts database: E1 has an RDS instance with storage_encrypted = true and a KMS key with rotation. E2 also mentions KMS-encrypted RDS. TLS is shown only at the public ingress (E3), which has a TLS secret, cert-manager and an ssl-redirect. The ingress forwards to the backend on port 8080, and nothing shows that this hop is encrypted. E1 names a "force-ssl" parameter group, but its contents aren't shown. No evidence covers encryption of logs (the Loki store in E10) or model artefacts, and the TLS minimum version (1.2+) isn't configured anywhere.
gaps: No evidence of encryption at rest for logs (Loki storage) or application log volumes
No evidence of encryption at rest for model artefacts (the model is an external API, so this may be N/A, but it is not documented)
TLS minimum version 1.2+ is not enforced or shown (no ssl-protocols or ssl_min_protocol_version setting)
Ingress-to-service traffic on port 8080 is not shown to use TLS or mTLS
The force-ssl RDS parameter group definition is not shown, so DB connection TLS is unverified
Outbound traffic to the OpenAI API and the Loki shipping path are not shown to use TLS
verdicts.remediation: Add Terraform for the log storage (Loki backend, S3 or EBS) with SSE-KMS or encrypted = true. Document whether model artefacts exist and how they are encrypted. In the ingress-nginx ConfigMap, set ssl-protocols to "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3". Add a service mesh or in-cluster TLS for the ingress-to-backend hop. Include the postgres16-force-ssl parameter group in the repo with rds.force_ssl=1 and ssl_min_protocol_version=TLSv1.2. Document that outbound calls (OpenAI, Loki) use HTTPS.

verdicts.rationale: The evidence supports most of the requirement. /api/chat is declared public in config/app.yaml (E3). It is rate-limited (E2) and also requires a signed session token (E1, E2). The admin transcript route uses requireAdmin, which checks the `support-admin` role from an RS256-verified SSO token (E1, E2). However, the index.ts excerpt (E2) is truncated at the admin route. The imports include deleteCustomerData and startRetentionJob, and E1 says erasure needs admin. I can't see the erasure route or any others, such as model reload or threshold changes, so I can't confirm that every route is protected. Because the route enumeration is incomplete, I can't mark it fully compliant.
gaps: The route list in server/src/index.ts is truncated, so the full set of routes can't be enumerated
The erasure route (deleteCustomerData) isn't visible, so its requireAdmin protection can't be confirmed
No evidence on whether model reload or threshold-change endpoints exist or are protected
The ingress exposes only /api/chat, but there is no evidence of network-level protection for /admin
verdicts.remediation: Review the complete server/src/index.ts and any other routers to confirm that every non-chat route, including the erasure route and any model or threshold admin routes, uses requireAdmin. Add a route-level test that fails if an undeclared route lacks authentication. Keep /api/chat as the only entry in public_endpoints.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to high risk systems; this system is classified as limited.

MODEL_CARD.md exists (E1) and covers provider/model, owner, intended and out-of-scope use, product-specific evaluation metrics and limitations, so the file-exists check passes. It is missing a training data summary. For a third-party model, the policy asks for the provider, the model version and a product-specific evaluation. The card's version is only the alias `gpt-4o-mini`, "pinned via LLM_MODEL". The code defaults to the same alias (E3, E10). The logs show a dated snapshot, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 (E6), which the card doesn't record. The card also appears to cover only one deployed model, which seems to be the only one in the repo (E10, E11).
gaps: No training data summary (even a pointer to the provider's documentation and a statement that no fine-tuning or own training data is used, as in the ADR)
Exact model version/snapshot not stated; only the alias gpt-4o-mini, while logs show gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18
No card version or date for the card itself
The embedding model used for retrieval (E4) is not covered by a card, if it counts as a deployed model
verdicts.remediation: Update MODEL_CARD.md. Add a "Training data" section saying the model is third-party, with a link to OpenAI's documentation, and that no fine-tuning is done (see ADR 0001); the only own data is the help-centre content used for retrieval. Record the pinned snapshot (e.g. gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18) and pin it in config/app.yaml and LLM_MODEL instead of the floating alias. Add a card version and date. Add a card, or a section, for the embedding model if it is deployed in production.

verdicts.rationale: The public AI endpoint /api/chat (E1, E3, E5) is protected by express-rate-limit (E3, E6). The limit comes from configuration (rate_limit.chat_per_minute: 20 in E1, read via cfg in E3). It is applied per client, keyed on x-session-id or IP (E3). The log shows the limiter firing ("rate limit exceeded", E8), and the ROPA lists rate limiting as a security measure (E4).
gaps: The key uses the client-supplied x-session-id header, which is unauthenticated and rotatable. A client could bypass the limit by sending a new value on each request.
The limiter runs before sessionAuth, so the key is not the verified session or API key.
No ingress or gateway throttling annotation is present (E5). This is defence in depth rather than a requirement.
Behind the ingress, req.ip may be the proxy address unless 'trust proxy' is set. This is not shown in the excerpts.
verdicts.remediation: Key the limiter on the verified session id (res.locals.sessionId) after sessionAuth, or combine it with req.ip. Do not use the raw x-session-id header. Set app.set('trust proxy', ...) correctly for the ingress. Optionally add nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps annotations to infra/k8s/ingress.yaml as a second layer.

verdicts.rationale: E1 (docs/incident-response.md) is an AI-specific incident response procedure. It covers detection (harmful-reply classifier alerts, handover spikes, complaints tagged ai-answer), containment, escalation (Customer Care lead, #supportbot-incidents) and reporting. It requires serious incidents (harmful or discriminatory output, personal data leak through the model) to be reported to the AI Governance Board at ai-incidents@acme.example within 24 hours. E2 confirms the document is part of the repository layout.
gaps: Policy also lists significant performance degradation and safety events as AI incidents. The procedure's serious-incident examples don't name them.
The 24-hour clock is not stated as starting at detection.
verdicts.remediation: Optionally update docs/incident-response.md. Add performance degradation and safety events to the incident categories, and state that the 24-hour reporting window starts at detection.

verdicts.rationale: Applies to high risk systems; this system is classified as limited.

# Model card: SupportBot answer generation

* **Provider / model:** OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini` (API, EU data residency), pinned via `LLM_MODEL`.
* **Owner:** Customer Care Engineering (care-eng@acme.example).
* **Intended use:** answering customer questions on orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs using
  retrieved help-centre extracts; handing over to a human agent.
* **Out of scope:** legal, financial or energy-saving advice; contract changes; complaints decisions.
* **Product evaluation (2026-08, 600 labelled conversations):** answer correctness 91.3%, grounded
  in retrieved context 95.0%, correct handover 88.0%, harmful/off-policy replies 0.3%.
* **Limitations:** may hallucinate tariff details not in the help centre; English and German only.

# SupportBot

Customer-support assistant for the ACME Home Energy web shop. The widget answers questions about
orders, deliveries, invoices and tariffs using an LLM (OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini`) grounded on our help
centre articles, and hands over to a human agent on request.

## AI Act position
SupportBot is a chatbot that interacts directly with customers. It does not take decisions about
people and is not in any Annex III area, so it is a **limited-risk** system: the transparency
obligations of Art. 50 apply (users must know they are talking to an AI).

## Layout
| Path | |
|---|---|
| `server/` | Express + TypeScript API (`/api/chat`, admin transcript tools) |
| `web/` | Chat widget (React) embedded in the shop |
| `config/app.yaml` | rate limits, retention, model settings |
| `infra/` | Terraform (RDS Postgres) and Kubernetes manifests |
| `docs/` | privacy notice, record of processing, incident response, ADRs |

# Privacy notice: support chat

**Controller:** ACME Home Energy GmbH, Hauptstr. 5, 10115 Berlin. DPO: privacy@acme-energy.example.

**Purpose and legal basis.** We process your chat messages to answer your support request
(Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR, performance of your contract) and to improve answer quality and handle
complaints (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, legitimate interest).

**AI assistant.** Replies are generated by an AI assistant operated on our behalf by OpenAI Ireland
Ltd. (processor). You can ask for a human agent at any time.

**Recipients.** OpenAI (processor, EU region), our customer-care team.

**Retention.** Chat transcripts are stored for 2 years and then deleted automatically.

**Your rights.** Right of access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, portability and
the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority. Contact privacy@acme-energy.example.

# Record of processing activities: SupportBot (entry PA-CC-07)

| Item | Content |
|---|---|
| Controller | ACME Home Energy GmbH; DPO privacy@acme-energy.example |
| Purposes | Customer support via chat; quality assurance; complaint handling |
| Data subjects | Customers and prospective customers using the chat |
| Personal data | Chat messages (free text, may contain contact and contract data), customer id, session id |
| Recipients | Customer-care team; OpenAI Ireland Ltd. (processor) |
| Transfers | None outside the EEA (EU data residency contract) |
| Erasure time limits | Transcripts 2 years; application logs 90 days |
| Security measures | TLS, KMS-encrypted RDS, admin RBAC, rate limiting |

port: 8080
llm:
  provider: openai
  model: gpt-4o-mini
public_endpoints:
  - /api/chat
rate_limit:
  chat_per_minute: 20
retention:
  transcript_days: 730     # 2 years: QA sampling and complaint handling
logging:
  sink: loki
  retention_days: 90

resource "aws_kms_key" "supportbot" {
  description         = "SupportBot data key"
  enable_key_rotation = true
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "transcripts" {
  identifier                 = "supportbot-transcripts"
  engine                     = "postgres"
  engine_version             = "16.3"
  instance_class             = "db.t4g.medium"
  allocated_storage          = 100
  storage_encrypted          = true
  kms_key_id                 = aws_kms_key.supportbot.arn
  db_subnet_group_name       = "private-data"
  publicly_accessible        = false
  backup_retention_period    = 7
  deletion_protection        = true
  parameter_group_name       = "postgres16-force-ssl"
}

# ADR 0001: Use a hosted LLM with retrieval instead of fine-tuning

* Status: accepted (2026-02-11)

We use OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini` through the API with EU data residency and zero data retention on the
provider side, grounded with help-centre extracts (top-4 BM25 + embeddings). Fine-tuning was
rejected: help-centre content changes weekly. Customer messages are sent to the provider as typed;
redaction of contact details was evaluated but postponed because it reduced answer quality for
delivery questions.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: supportbot
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [support-api.acme-energy.example]
      secretName: supportbot-tls
  rules:
    - host: support-api.acme-energy.example
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api/chat
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: {service: {name: supportbot, port: {number: 8080}}}

# AI incident response

1. **Detect:** alerts on harmful-reply classifier hits, spikes in handover rate, customer complaints
   tagged `ai-answer`.
2. **Contain:** on-call engineer can switch the widget to "human agents only" via the feature flag
   `chat.ai_enabled`.
3. **Escalate:** notify Customer Care lead and #supportbot-incidents.
4. **Report:** serious incidents (harmful or discriminatory output, personal data leak through the
   model) are reported to the AI Governance Board at ai-incidents@acme.example within 24 hours;
   personal data breaches also go to the DPO for the 72-hour GDPR assessment.
5. **Review:** blameless post-mortem within 10 working days.
